summary:
Enugu State lies wholly within Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide and reaches conduct well beyond marriage: cohabitation between same-sex partners, public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment. Human Rights Watch records that police have invoked the Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrest. Trans identity is not expressly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed through that enforcement culture.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's updated travel advice, as reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation. It states that same-sex conduct carries up to 14 years' imprisonment, that some northern states apply Sharia provisions capable of prescribing the death penalty, and that the same-sex marriage law reaches those who help arrange or attend such weddings. Enugu State is not among the Sharia states, so the death-penalty layer does not apply there.

Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report documents the Act's operation in Enugu State itself. Sharon, a bisexual woman from Enugu State, told the researchers that she married a male friend from high school in July 2015 under family and social pressure and that for as long as she remained in Nigeria she would stay married. The finding illustrates how the statute's prohibition of same-sex partnership pushes people into heterosexual marriages rather than merely punishing them.

Healthcare access is a documented gap in Enugu State. An activist based in Enugu told Human Rights Watch that the major challenge in the state is the rate of HIV and STIs among community members, and that there are no clinics where gay men and men who have sex with men can obtain services without fear of harassment. Many therefore travel to Lagos and other states for care, a journey that itself requires disclosure and carries exposure.

Violence risk for visitors remains elevated across the country. Police have used the Act to stop, beat and extort men perceived as gay, and kito gangs lure LGBTQ+ people through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. Dating-app use in Enugu therefore carries the same entrapment risk documented elsewhere in Nigeria.
tangentialFactors:
The only trans-specific imprisonment case in the source set concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), sentenced on 12 April 2024 to six months for naira abuse and held in a maximum-security prison in Lagos. An October 2024 investigative panel found that housing her there violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender, and press coverage at sentencing openly debated which prison would hold her, indicating that placement between male and female sections is left to official discretion. The case indicates how a trans prisoner's placement may be decided in Nigerian custody generally.

In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, the TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja. Police described the deceased as a man dressed in female clothing. Six months later, in February 2025, no suspects had been charged. Official indifference to killings of trans people is documented at national level.

Northern states are the point of sharpest divergence from Enugu: Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. Southern states including Enugu face the secular penalty only.
localsOnly:
Residents of Enugu State live under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 as federal criminal law, with penalties of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct and for organising, promoting or attending same-sex weddings. Nigeria offers no legal protections on sexual orientation or gender identity, and the Act reinforced colonial-era criminalisation.

Human Rights Watch's October 2016 fieldwork in Enugu State recorded a bisexual woman, Sharon, entering a heterosexual marriage in July 2015 under family and social pressure, and an Enugu activist reporting that HIV and STI rates are the leading community health problem, with no clinic in the state where gay men and men who have sex with men can be seen without fear of harassment. Service users travel to Lagos and other states for testing and treatment.

Press coverage of Bobrisky's April 2024 sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep her in, and prison placement between male and female sections appears to rest with the Nigerian Correctional Service's discretion rather than any published rule.
outOfScopeNotes:
Reuters reported in September 2022 that transgender Nigerians feared proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public. Whether any such proposal has been enacted is unresolved in the sources available here.

No Enugu State-specific prosecutions, arrests or police operations under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act are documented in this inventory; the state-level evidence consists of the Human Rights Watch interviews on marriage pressure and clinic access. Enforcement patterns cited are drawn from Lagos and Abuja and are indicative rather than Enugu-specific.
